paper_title: VoxLock: Target-Speaker Extraction for Voice Agents Without an Enrollment Step

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A voice agent's speech recognizer transcribes everyone near the microphone, including people other than the caller. I fine-tuned a public causal target-speaker extraction model (REAL-TSE, 27M parameters) on one GPU to work from a voice sample cut from the call itself, and released it as VoxLock. I score it by what a recognizer writes on real recordings. On Krisp's 265-recording benchmark it reaches 4.95% WER against 23.21% unprocessed and lets 9 background words into the transcript over 85 minutes of background-only speech. Its WER is not significantly different from Krisp's best filters and is significantly lower than the other commercial and open systems I tested. On 400 AMI meeting windows built and frozen before scoring, it cuts WER from 42.95% to 10.63%. The 8-bit model runs a live call on 77% of one CPU thread with 24 ms of algorithmic latency. Model, code and per-file scores are open.

sections.content: 2. Model, code and per-file scores are open. Index Terms: target speaker extraction, voice isolation, voice agents, speech recognition, streaming 1. Introduction Voice agents hear whoever is near the microphone: coworker at the next desk, television, second person in the car. What they say ends up in the transcript, and the agent answers it. Noise suppressors do not help because they are built to keep speech. Krisp, ai-coustics and Sanas sell voice isolation filters for this, but they are closed and licensed per minute or per device. Target-speaker extraction (TSE) is the research version of the same problem: given mixture and short enrollment recording of one speaker, output only that speaker [1, 2, 3]. Two things keep it out of voice agents. An agent has no enrollment recording, only the call. And TSE papers usually report signal metrics on simulated mixtures, while an agent cares about what the recognizer writes on real audio. VoxLock is my attempt to close that gap with one GPU. This paper covers: taking the voice sample from the call itself, so the agent passes in one audio stream; fine-tuning public causal TSE baseline [4] on one NVIDIA L4; scoring recognizer output against seven models from three commercial vendors and five open models, on Krisps benchmark, 134 AMI windows, and 400 AMI windows frozen before scoring; releasing the runtime (VoxLock 1.2.1), which runs live call on one CPU thread. SpeakerBeam [1] and VoiceFilter [2] condition separator on an embedding of an enrollment utterance. VoiceFilter-Lite [5] made this streaming and on-device for recognition. The personalized track of the DNS challenges [6] uses pre-recorded enrollment clip. Lin et al. [7] take the speaker cue from the mixture itself instead, using distance to find the near talker. Band-split RNNs (BSRNN) [8] were extended to personalized enhancement [9] and are the TSE backbone in WeSep [10]. REAL-T [11] and the REAL-TSE challenge [4] moved evaluation to real conversations and released causal BSRNN baselines; VoxLock starts from one. Separation models such as TIGER [12] and SAM Audio [13] output several sources without knowing which is the caller, and noise suppressors such as DeepFilterNet [14] keep all speech. did not find published work comparing open TSE with commercial voice-isolation products on real recordings by downstream recognition. 3. Method 3.1. Model The starting point is the causal tfmap_context BSRNN from the REAL-TSE baseline in WeSep [10, 4]: 16 kHz audio, 512-sample STFT, 128-sample hop, six band-split blocks and unidirectional sequence modeling, 27M parameters. Its author confirmed that the parameters he trained are released under Apache-2.0. The voice sample enters twice. First, each frame of the calls spectrum attends over the frames of the samples spectrum, giving an extra input channel. Second, the separators band features attend over frame-level ECAPA-TDNN [15] features of the sample, and the result multiplies into each band. Algorithmic latency is 24 ms, the 512-sample window minus the 128-sample hop. 3.2. Voice sample from the call The model takes exactly 3 of the caller. For recording use the loudest 3 in the first 15 s, so whole-file run looks up to 15 ahead for its sample. For live stream, audio passes through unchanged until 3 of speech have been heard, counting 10 ms frames at least 10 dB above the quietest frame of the last 2 s; those become the sample and isolation starts. Both rules assume the caller is the loudest, earliest talker, which holds for headset or phone held by the caller. 3.3. Training Every stage minimizes negative SI-SDR [16] with AdamW (weight decay 0.01, gradient clip 5), trains all weights including the ECAPA-TDNN branch, and starts from the previous one  (Table 4)  . The learning rate is 104 in S1 (cosine) and S2, decaying to 105 over the last 1,000 steps of S2, and 3 105 in S3 and S4. S1, simulated calls (4,000 steps, 6 examples). near-field LibriSpeech [17] caller is mixed with one or two background talkers, usually 015 dB quieter, in half the examples as close as the caller and otherwise 1.55 away in simulated rooms; 25% of examples go through telephone channel. The voice sample is the first 3 of the mixture or another utterance of the caller, clean or noisy. S2, real crosstalk (4,000 steps). Each step adds batch of AMI headset audio [18] from 40 meetings to the simulated batch. headset records its wearer and, more quietly, everyone else. For the first 1,000 steps the real batch is 4 windows where the wearer talks alone, an exact target, plus the same headsets crosstalk from moments when only others talk, at 012 dB above its natural level. For the remaining 3,000 steps it is 8 of that crosstalk alone with 34 caller clip pasted in, the target silent outside the clip. No meeting from the evaluation sets or from REAL-T is used. S3, long calls (800 steps, 30 examples). Trained on 6 windows, the model let caller who talks without pause fade by 20 dB within 40 s. S3 trains on 30 examples, most with continuous caller. S4, distance and room (400 steps). The model had learned to keep whichever talker was closer. S4 places the caller near, mid or far independently of the background talkers and adds real AMI room tone. S3 and S4 keep the real batch at half weight. 4. Evaluation Krisp benchmark [19]: 265 real recordings of main talker with second voice in the room (work, call center, phone calls), with transcripts and speaker segment times. Krisp publishes the outputs of its VI 2.5 models, which score as released. AMI: 134 windows from five meetings and seven people, with the headset wearer as the caller: ES2003ad from AMIs training partition and IS1008a from its development partition, none of them used in my training. looked at both sets during development: AMI picked among S2 checkpoints, and Krisp exposed the problems S3 and S4 fix. So neither is blind. Blind AMI: after the model was final, ran the same script on the 19 AMI meetings REAL-T uses for evaluation. Eight failed to download, so the 400 windows (16 people) come from 11 meetings, all in AMIs standard test partition. froze them by hash before running any model. Each AMI window starts at 315 turn of the wearer and runs 4 past it while others talk, so the caller always speaks first, which suits sample taken from the start. Transcripts come from Parakeet TDT 0.6B [20] (v2 on Krisp with Krisps published text normalization, v3 on AMI). report three metrics: WER on the callers words; missed, (𝑆 + 𝐷)/𝑁, the share of the callers words the transcript loses; and leak, the number of recognized words whose midpoint falls where only background speech is present (more than 0.25 from caller speech), per minute of such audio. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over people (5,000 draws), uncorrected for multiple comparisons. People in the same meeting are not independent, so the AMI intervals are, if anything, too narrow. compare against Krisp VI 2.5 (four models), ai-coustics Voice Focus 2.2 and (local SDK), Sanas Voice Isolation SE 1.0 (cloud SDK, fed in real time), Hush [21], DeepFilterNet3 [14], TIGER [12] (in 10 chunks, keeping the output whose ECAPA embedding is closest to the first 3 of speech), SAM Audio small [13] (a text prompt plus the first 3 of speech Table 1: Krisp benchmark, 265 real recordings. Commercial versions are those available in October 2026. VoxLock rows are the float32 model on the whole file unless stated. The commercial filters run causally, so Table 1 also gives live(), which does too. 5. Results Krisp benchmark  (Table 1)  . VoxLock and Krisp Default are not significantly different on WER, missed words or leak. Krisp Balanced is not significantly different on WER or missed words but leaks significantly more. Against Krisp HD the WER difference is borderline, with an interval starting at +0.01. VoxLock has significantly lower WER than Krisp Lite, both ai-coustics models, Sanas and every open model. Run causally with live(), VoxLock scores 5.15%, still below Krisp Defaults 5.30%. In counts, 9 background words reached the VoxLock transcript in 85.3 minutes of background-only speech, against 130 for Krisp Default and 5,674 unprocessed. There is cost when there is nothing to remove. In the phone-call scenario, which has almost no background speech, VoxLock raises WER from 3.82% to 5.36% (Krisp Default: 4.15%), while in the work and call-center scenarios it lowers WER from 29.31% and 25.13% to 4.83% and 4.90%. On 200 windows where only the caller talks, from the 19 blind-set meetings (20 people), VoxLocks WER is 0.31 points above unprocessed audio (7.49% against 7.18%; interval [0.32, +1.33], not significant). With seven people the intervals are wide. Blind AMI  (Table 3)  . On windows nobody looked at during development, VoxLock cuts WER from 42.95% to 10.63% and leaked words from 98 to 1.2 per minute. Taking the sample from the first 3 of speech, found with Silero VAD [22], instead of the loudest 3 makes no significant difference here; on Krisp it raises WER by 0.13 points [+0.01, +0.28]. The live path passes each window through unprocessed until it has heard 3 of speech. Other systems are missing from this set: no longer have the ai-coustics key used for Table 2, Krisp publishes outputs only for its own benchmark, and did not run Sanas or the open baselines on it. Does it use the voice sample? When the voice sample is 3 turn of another person from the same meeting, the REALTSE checkpoint follows that person and loses 61% of the callers words. VoxLock loses 17% (8% with the right sample). So it does use the sample, but it also learned to keep the dominant near-field talker, and wrong sample degrades it instead of flipping it to the other person. Stages  (Table 4)  . Most of the gain comes from S1: Krisp WER drops from 9.99% to 5.61% and blind AMI from 14.75% to 11.07%. After S1, blind AMI WER moves by at most 0.6 points, and S1, S2 and S3 are not significantly different from VoxLock there. Blind AMI windows are 719 of headset audio, so the long-call fade and the distance shortcut that S3 and S4 fix rarely come up in them. The later stages matter on Krisp, where leak falls from 2.25 to 0.11 words per minute and WER from 5.61% to 4.95% (both significant). cannot credit real crosstalk alone for this: the first 1,000 steps of S2 were no better than 1,000 more simulated steps, and leaked significantly 6. Deployment VoxLock 1.2.1 runs the model as two ONNX graphs. The enroll graph runs once per call on the voice sample and returns its normalized spectrum and, for every band, the keys and values of the attention over the samples features. The chunk graph runs on each chunk of the call with those tensors and the recurrent state, so per chunk it does only work that depends on the call. In float32, streaming output equals whole-file pass up to float rounding. The 8-bit model (recurrent layers quantized) scores 5.11% WER on Krisp. measured CPU load on 60 call as process CPU time over audio time, Python loop included, with one onnxruntime 1.31.1 thread on Google Cloud g2-standard-8 (Intel Xeon, 2.2 GHz). In 80 ms chunks the call uses 61% of the thread, in 40 ms chunks 77%, and in 20 ms chunks 110%, more than one thread has; on two threads, 20 ms chunks run at 0.86 times real time (wall clock). These figures are for steady streaming and leave out the switch described below. Delay is the chunk length plus the 24 ms algorithmic latency. On an NVIDIA L4 the float32 model processes recording 40 times faster than real time. At the switch from pass-through to isolation, live() first runs the network over the call so far (up to 30 s) and drops that output, so the recurrent state has heard the call from its start instead of beginning mid-sentence. This costs 25 of compute on one CPU thread, once per call. It runs inside the push() that completes the voice sample, so on one thread the output stalls for that long at the switch and then lags until it has caught up. On Krisp, live() scores 5.15% WER against 4.95% for the same model on the whole file. 7. Limitations The model is English-trained, 16 kHz and single-caller. The automatic voice sample assumes the caller is the loudest early if background talker dominates the first seconds, talker; VoxLock keeps the wrong person. Both comparison sets were seen during development, and every AMI window starts with the caller, which suits the automatic sample. The Krisp benchmark comes from vendor whose systems compare against; its license (CC BY-NC 4.0) rules out commercial use. All transcripts come from one recognizer family, and all results from one training run. 8. Conclusion public TSE baseline, fine-tuned on one GPU and given voice sample from the call, removes background voices for recognizer about as well as Krisps best filters tested, and with lower WER than every other system holds up on blind set of meetings, and runs live on one CPU thread. The model, ONNX graphs, Python package and per-file evaluation scores are at https:// github.com/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock and https: //huggingface.co/arbazsiddiqui/voxlock.
